```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
```

## The question

In 2011, Derrick Rose became the youngest MVP in NBA history at just 22 years old, winning 113 of 121 first-place votes after leading the Chicago Bulls to the league's best record (62-20). However, the award is still debated today, because other players, especially LeBron James, put up stronger numbers that season. In this report, I use MVP voting data and regression analysis to test whether Rose's MVP was backed up by the stats, or whether something else drove the voters.

## The data

Data comes from Basketball-Reference: official MVP voting results (with each candidate's stats) and team ratings for the 2005-06 through 2014-15 seasons.

```{r load-data}
mvp <- read_csv("data/mvp_2011.csv")

mvp <- mvp |>
  select(-`-9999`) |>
  rename(
    pts_won = `Pts Won`,
    pts_max = `Pts Max`,
    fg_pct  = `FG%`,
    fg3_pct = `3P%`,
    ft_pct  = `FT%`,
    ws_48   = `WS/48`
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Rank    = parse_number(Rank),
    is_rose = Player == "Derrick Rose"
  )
```

## How Rose compared to other candidates

Rose ranked 4th in Win Shares and 6th in scoring among the 13 players who received MVP votes, yet he received 98% of the possible vote points.

```{r chart-win-shares}
ggplot(mvp, aes(x = WS, y = reorder(Player, WS), fill = is_rose)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#2a78d6", "FALSE" = "grey70"), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Rose ranked 4th in Win Shares among MVP vote-getters",
    x = "Win Shares",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r chart-points}
ggplot(mvp, aes(x = PTS, y = reorder(Player, PTS), fill = is_rose)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#2a78d6", "FALSE" = "grey70"), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Rose ranked 6th in scoring among MVP vote-getters",
    x = "Points per game",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r chart-scatter}
ggplot(mvp, aes(x = WS, y = Share, color = is_rose)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = Player), size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#2a78d6", "FALSE" = "grey50"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Rose won 98% of the vote share despite ranking 4th in Win Shares",
    x = "Win Shares",
    y = "MVP vote share"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## What do MVP voters usually reward?

To learn what voters typically reward, I trained regression models on nine other seasons of MVP voting (2006-2015, excluding 2011), then used them to predict the 2011 vote.

```{r load-all-seasons}
files <- list.files("data", pattern = "^mvp_\\d{4}\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

all_mvp <- read_csv(files, id = "file") |>
  select(-`-9999`) |>
  rename(
    pts_won = `Pts Won`,
    pts_max = `Pts Max`,
    fg_pct  = `FG%`,
    fg3_pct = `3P%`,
    ft_pct  = `FT%`,
    ws_48   = `WS/48`
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Rank   = parse_number(Rank),
    season = parse_number(file)
  )

team_files <- list.files("data", pattern = "^teams_\\d{4}\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

teams <- read_csv(team_files, id = "file") |>
  mutate(
    season = parse_number(file),
    Team   = str_remove(Team, "\\*")
  ) |>
  select(season, Team, W, L, MOV)

abbrevs <- read_csv("data/team_abbrevs.csv")

all_mvp <- all_mvp |>
  left_join(abbrevs, by = "Tm") |>
  left_join(teams, by = c("season", "Team"))

# Drop players traded mid-season (team = "TOT"), since they have no single team record
all_mvp <- all_mvp |>
  filter(!is.na(W)) |>
  mutate(win_pct = W / (W + L))

# How many teammates also received MVP votes that season?
all_mvp <- all_mvp |>
  group_by(season, Tm) |>
  mutate(teammates_voted = n() - 1) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r models}
train <- all_mvp |> filter(season != 2011)
test  <- all_mvp |> filter(season == 2011)

model1 <- lm(Share ~ WS, data = train)                              # Win Shares only
model2 <- lm(Share ~ WS + Age, data = train)                        # + age (not significant)
model3 <- lm(Share ~ WS + W, data = train)                          # + team wins
model4 <- lm(Share ~ WS + win_pct, data = train)                    # + team win %
model5 <- lm(Share ~ WS + win_pct + teammates_voted, data = train)  # + teammates who got votes

rose <- test |> filter(Player == "Derrick Rose")

model_comparison <- tibble(
  model = c("1: WS", "2: WS + age", "3: WS + team wins",
            "4: WS + win %", "5: WS + win % + teammates"),
  adj_r2 = c(summary(model1)$adj.r.squared,
             summary(model2)$adj.r.squared,
             summary(model3)$adj.r.squared,
             summary(model4)$adj.r.squared,
             summary(model5)$adj.r.squared),
  rose_predicted = c(predict(model1, rose),
                     predict(model2, rose),
                     predict(model3, rose),
                     predict(model4, rose),
                     predict(model5, rose))
) |>
  mutate(rose_gap = rose$Share - rose_predicted)

knitr::kable(model_comparison, digits = 3)
```

```{r predictions-2011}
test |>
  mutate(predicted = predict(model4, newdata = test)) |>
  select(Player, WS, win_pct, Share, predicted) |>
  arrange(desc(predicted)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Win Shares was the strongest predictor of vote share, and team win percentage also mattered; age did not. Even after accounting for Win Shares, team win percentage, and teammates splitting votes, the model predicted Rose would receive 39% of the vote share. Instead, he got 98%. Something beyond the stats, most likely the story of a 22-year-old leading his hometown team to the league's best record, drove voters in 2011.

## Comparing Rose to other MVP winners

```{r winners}
all_mvp |>
  filter(Rank == 1) |>
  select(season, Player, WS, ws_48, win_pct) |>
  arrange(WS) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Rose's 13.1 Win Shares is the second-lowest among the ten MVP winners from 2006 to 2015. LeBron's 15.6 would have been close to a typical MVP total.

## Conclusion

Based on what voters typically reward, LeBron James was the stronger MVP choice: he led every statistic I examined, his season was in line with past MVP winners, and my model gave him the highest predicted vote share (44.5% vs. Rose's 34.9%). Rose's MVP was earned through team success and a compelling story, but not through the numbers.
